newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crisis in fifth month, hopes on secret talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru crisis in fifth month, hopes on secret talks.

text.p: Peru's hostage crisis entered its fifth month on Thursday, with hopes for the safe release of 72 VIP captives pinned on frenetic behind-the-scenes talks between the key players.

More than 17 weeks after a band of jungle-trained gunmen burst into a lavish cocktail party at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, Peru's Episcopal Conference described the siege as "an open wound which hurts the whole country."
A three-man team overseeing crisis talks continued its daily shuttle diplomacy between the government and the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels on Wednesday.
The intense meetings, cloaked in secrecy, have led to some speculation that the announcement of a negotiated settlement is imminent.
However, a poll published this week showed that most Peruvians thought the standoff -- already the longest hostage situation in Latin America's history -- could drag on for months.
"It's idle to bet either way. At this stage it's just impossible to say when this could end," one Western diplomat said. "No one would ever have imagined it going on this long in the first place."

The main sticking point remains the MRTA demand for the release of hundreds of jailed comrades. President Alberto Fujimori has publicly ruled out this demand although sources close to the talks suggest the government may be prepared to free some lesser MRTA prisoners to avoid bloodshed.
Fujimori has already arranged asylum for the 20-odd hostage takers in Cuba and the Dominican Republic in the event of a peaceful solution.

While the MRTA's Dec. 17 assault on the residence astounded the world and dominated headlines in its early weeks, the tension and interest dissipated as it became clear that it was in neither side's interest to harm the hostages.

The MRTA, who have mined and booby trapped the diplomatic compound, initially seized more than 500 guests at the party but quickly released most. They hung on to those they considered most valuable, including the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen, two government ministers and Fujimori's younger brother.
A brief war of brinkmanship, which saw police circle the property in armoured vehicles and the MRTA firing warning shots into the air, has long since died down.
Only a bizarre daily musical war remains, with police drowning out early morning revolutionary anthems broadcast from the residence with battle tunes blasted from speakers surrounding the compound.

The 72 hostages who remain are all men and are mostly middle aged. They sleep on thin mattresses on the floor, eat food brought twice daily by the Red Cross, read, play cards and board games and exercise. Electricity, telephones and running water were cut off to the building at the start of the crisis.
Many are said to be suffering from stress-related illnesses such as high blood pressure, heart and stomach problems and receive almost daily medical attention.

The 121-day crisis has also taken its toll on those outside the residence. A mobile clinic was set up in an adjoining street Wednesday to attend to the hundreds of police and journalists who maintain a round-the-clock vigil at the site.
